The Scottish breeders, accompanied by Domenico Manzoni, returned to Italy on several other occasions until the 1980s, making repeated purchases of heifers and bulls that included, each time, 20 to 30 subjects. These visits allowed me to deepen my approach to the international environment of the breed, with which I maintained contacts that would prove important for my experiences as a technician and judge in the following years.

In the meantime, technology was making giant strides and, starting from the 1970s, the storage and use of frozen semen had become a reality, while the embryo transfer technique also appeared. This allowed Scottish breeders, also aided by a favorable health status, to export the genetics of the breed to Ireland, the USA, New Zealand and other countries, becoming a sort of springboard for the spread of the Romagnola throughout the world.

My beginning as a breed classifier

In 1976, just after obtaining my Agricultural diploma and before starting my studies in Veterinary Medicine at the University of Bologna, I was enrolled by Dr. Gian Marco Casadei, at the time director of the Provincial Breeders Association of Ravenna, in the first theoretical and practical course for Breed Classifiers organized by Anabic, which took place in Foligno, Umbria, in September of that same year and which I completed two years later, in 1978, becoming qualified for the Romagnola breed. This gave me the opportunity to carry out the first visual evaluations, to act as an assistant at National Shows and to act as a judge in local and provincial events. I completed my university studies by graduating in 1982, discussing an experimental thesis on the morphometric evolution of the Romagnola breed with Prof. Adalberto Falaschini as supervisor. After an apprenticeship in Faenza, with Dr. Giacomo Cimatti, a wellknown veterinary surgeon, and after a very short period of technical training at a feed company, I was hired in 1984 by a dairy industry in Bologna, working at the Ravenna Milk Producer Coop as in charge of milk quality control and mastitis prophylaxis in the herds of the contributing members in the provinces of Ravenna, Forlì and Rimini, until 1995. This period brought me closer to the world of dairy cows, in particular the Holstein Friesian breed, visiting farms, participating in conferences and Shows, learning about breeding technology, morphological and genetic evaluation criteria, as well as meeting classifiers and technicians. One of the latter, Corrado Zilocchi, passionate and capable co-owner of an important Holstein herd in the province of Mantua as well as head of the ANAFI Evaluations and Exhibition Service, has become, over time, a close friend. During these events, my frequentation of the Romagnola breed remained assiduous, as well as that of classifier and judge. To tell the truth, during the early 80s, my relations with Anabic, which at the time was still based in Rome, were rather difficult. The president was Enzo Saragoni, also president of the Provincial Breeders Association of Forlì, the director was Dr. Alberto Viganò, while the breed classifiers were handled by Romano Aliffi, previously a zootechnical controller at the Ascoli Piceno Breeders Association. It didn’t take me long to realize that the difficulties I encountered were not due to any shortcomings on my part but rather to the fact that, being close to Dr. Guberti, I automatically found myself in the opposite faction to the one that was dominant in those years.

In fact, the Provincial Breeders Association of Forlì dominated the Romagnola scene at the time, an active and efficient entity that not only had the highest number of animals registered in the Book, compared to other provinces in the breeding area, but that also managed, since 1968, its own AI Bull Center based in Diegaro di Cesena. The Saragoni presidency undoubtedly represented a period of growth for Anabic. The Ministry of Agriculture, in the era of Minister Marcora, granted substantial funding, which allowed the promotion of the Italian Beef Breeds in the major European exhibition events and beyond, giving them international visibility with important commercial implications. In 1982, the Consortium of Italian Beef “5R” was also established for the protection and promotion of meat produced from Italian breeds. Finally, in 1985, the Anabic Genetic Center was built, which arose in Boneggio, in the province of Perugia, on land donated to Anabic by the Umbria Region. The APA of Forlì, with Dr. Franco Mercuri as director and with Enzo Saragoni as vice-president, could not tolerate the competition of a private Center like that of Dr. Guberti who, without having any public funding, and therefore with his own resources, was able to consistently propose important sires, who received wide consensus not only in the province of Ravenna, but also in many Forlì herds, including the most important ones. As a thorn in the side of the prevailing system, Dr. Guberti was poorly tolerated and, together with him, his acolytes, of which I too, still very young, naive and largely unaware, was a part. Anabic fully supported, at all levels, the line of its president and, consequently, my career as an expert began on an uphill slope. This orientation translated into a not too veiled ostracism that I encountered both from Romano Aliffi, coordinator of the Anabic classifiers until 1988, and from Anteo Paterniani, from Pesaro and reference classifier for the Romagnola breed in the same years, to which I struggled to get used. If Romano Aliffi's coldness reflected the prevailing line, Anteo Paterniani's intolerance towards me emerged particularly during shows, where his meticulous and particularly slow approach clashed with mine, more instinctive and immediate. This attitude, which I believed I did not deserve, determined my progressive distancing from Anabic and from the body of assessors, which came close to becoming definitive.

Lucio Migni

The one who made me back down from my convictions was Lucio Migni, a young and passionate Chianina breeder, who arrived at Anabic in 1986, after a brief period of work at the University of Perugia. Lucio, born in 1963, agricultural technician, from Ospedalicchio, near Bastia Umbra, had been hired as a worker at the facilities of the testing station. I met him at the Forlì Show in September 1987, where I was exhibiting my pigeons and where he had intervened as a representative of Anabic. Lucio had seen part of my degree thesis, relating to the standard of the Romagnola breed and the illustrative drawings of the evaluation scheme, which had been published on “4 Razze”, Anabic’s magazine in those years. I had instead only heard of him as a “new acquisition” of Anabic. In Forlì we only had a brief exchange of words that gave me the impression of an empathetic, intelligent, direct and nice person, dissonant with respect to the environment that characterized the Anabic of the time. Later Lucio told me that he had noticed a certain nervousness in my attitude, indicative of the discomfort that I now felt towards the structure. In that period, although I continued to visit the herds, I had distanced myself from Anabic, dedicating myself to work and to my passion for pigeon shows, relating to the Autosexing Texan Pioneer breed, which I shared with some friends and which I cultivated for decades. My passion for animal husbandry and show pigeons also infected my flatmates during the university period, converting them to pigeon breeding, while two of them, Riccardo Franzoni and Alfredo Marchetti, were, for a certain period, also Romagnola breeders. Lucio Migni, understanding the reasons for my disaffection, began to involve me in various activities of the Association, convincing me to extend my qualification as a classifier to all five breeds and determining my progressive rapprochement with Anabic. My first evaluation rounds carried out in various provinces on the Chianina and Marchigiana breeds, the study tours on the Maremmana and Podolica breeds, the redefinition of the standards of the Italian breeds, the first choices of the bull calves entering the Testing Station and the debut in the ring of the major shows date back to the years between 1990 and 1994. I owe to Lucio, in particular, the deepening of my knowledge of the Chianina breed, my first experiences as an international judge for the Marchigiana and Chianina breeds and, last but not least, my arrival in Anabic, which took place in 1995.

The earliest international experiences

Another of my study companions, Fredrik “Fred” W.D. Garnum, a veterinarian, born in 1958 in Rome to Swedish parents, raised in various countries around the world with his family, receiving an international education and speaking several languages ​​fluently, has contributed significantly to broadening my horizons, both from a human and professional point of view. Visiting Romagna on several occasions, Fred, still a student, soon met Dr. Guberti and his Tori Center, as well as Corrado Giuliani and his family, becoming a regular visitor to the Romagnola herds. It can be said that Romagna and the Giuliani family have adopted him and, as also happened to Alfredo Marchetti, his friend since childhood, as well as a common classmate, he ended up settling there permanently, starting a family and practicing his profession as a veterinarian. Thanks to Fred, my relationships with international breeders have intensified. In fact, it was he who first met, in the summer of 1987, the Northern Irish Romagnola breeder Samuel “Uel” T. Kennedy, a young enthusiast of the breed who had come with his family to the Veterinary Faculty of Bologna in search of contacts, and who directed him to Romagna, where I accompanied him on a tour of visits to the herds. Only a year later, in 1988, I was invited by Uel, not without emotion, to judge the Romagnola at the Ballymena Show, in Ulster. It was the occasion to visit the Romagnola herds in Ireland and Scotland. The extraordinary quality of the cattle that I had the opportunity to inspect in the many herds that dotted the tour, gave me the confirmation that the breed had left its mark. The Scottish herds, Dunure of George Mc Ilwraith, Pirnhall of Donald Findlay, Knockdolian of Lord Richard Wellesley as well as the Northern Irish Tandragee Castle Estate, which had purchased the very valid scottish Stirling herd of John Hornall, left me speechless. The founders that had left Italy in the 70s (Caesar, Dritto, Binario, Marcus, Telstar) were no longer alive but their descendants were building very valid cattle. This first tour of the United Kingdom and Ireland was followed by others and in quick succession, between 1989 and 1991, I was invited to judge the Romagnola at the Rojal Dublin Show, the Balmoral Show in Belfast, and the Rojal Highland Show in Edinburgh, always finding, both at the show and in the herds, stock of great value. These were important experiences that would not have had the same consequences without the support of a globetrotter like Fred Garnum. From the conversations held with international breeders during these events it was clear that from Scotland the Romagnola had taken flight to numerous Countries, finding passionate supporters there. Our contacts in Ireland were the basis for the export of about thirty Romagnola breed heads and others of the Piemontese breed on behalf of the Northern Irish Tandragee Castle Estate and Uel Kennedy's Hazelwood herds. On this occasion the choice of subjects was taken care of by Corrado Giuliani and myself while the organization of the entire expedition, including the air embarkation to Ireland from Turin Caselle airport, was the work of Fred Garnum. Among the Romagnola cattle were some bulls such as Unno, Umberto, Ubero, Uranio and others, who would have a significant role in the following years both in Ireland and in other countries. In the meantime I was contacted by the American Romagnola Association, based in Alturas, California, to intervene in the 1990 edition of the National Show of the Romagnola USA in Reno, Nevada, with the aim of illustrating the characteristics of the breed and carrying out part of the judging. Fred and I flew to the US, where we were able to form a first favorable impression of the American Romagnola, confirmed in the following days by a tour of visits to the Californian herds, in which we were accompanied by the president of ARA, Joe T. Covington. On the same occasion we had the opportunity to observe the bull Swordale Marco, an interesting son of Prisco imported shortly before from Scotland. I returned enthusiastic and only 2 years later, in February 1992, I was invited to judge the Romagnola, which presented over 100 high quality exhibits, at the National Show in Houston, Texas, in the imposing setting of the Astrodome, one of the temples of the global beef industry. The show was followed by an interesting tour of visits to the herds that allowed us to establish in-depth contacts that developed in the following years.

The “Post Guberti” and Anabic’s new course

In the same period, in Italy, many things were changing. In 1987, the AI center of Dr. Giorgio Guberti had closed its doors and Romagnola had lost forever one of its main points of reference. In an attempt to stem this enormous loss, I, together with Fred Garnum, Alfredo Marchetti and Gianluca Giuliani, son of Corrado, proceeded to purchase the bull Macario, by Treno, of the Titano line, who had won many awards at shows, who we bought from the Rimini stud of Adolfo Pasini and who we took to the INFA University AI Center of Cadriano, near Bologna, for semen production. Shortly after, the bulls Tarcisio, son of Ivan from the Babini herd of Ravenna, and Azzurro, by Bolero born in the nucleus of the Fiorentini Bros in Forlì, also entered the same center. In the same years, continuing to evaluate the Romagnola breed as a classifier in the various provinces, I suggested to Dr. Mercuri, director of the APA of Forlì, to collect at the FA Center of Diegaro, now part of the Semenitaly group, the sires Otto, by Lamone, born in the Renzo Scozzoli Stud, and also Boy, by Vano raised in Ravenna by Gian Michele Graziani. In 1989 and 1990 the Diegaro center also purchased Lubio and Metro, both raised by the Fiorentini Bros. All these sires stemmed the emergency in an extremely delicate period for the breed. In those same years Anabic had renewed itself. Dr. Nicola Marcantonio, a Marchigiana breeder from Chieti, took over the presidency from Enzo Saragoni, while Dr. Guido Perosino, an agronomist from Turin, who came from the private sector, arrived to manage the structure in 1988, after the brief management of Dr. Gianni Salis. The change in leadership coincided with a real revolution for Anabic, which was transferred from its previous headquarters in Rome to its current headquarters in S. Martino in Colle, Perugia. The staff was strengthened with the hiring of new personnel and the Association's activity received a clear boost at all levels. The genetic center, which until then had played a marginal role, was the subject of a profound review of the performance test and its own activity, equipping itself to become the linchpin of selective activity for Italian breeds. To reaffirm its central role, the Central Technical Commission of the Herd Book established that, starting from June 1990, only performance-tested sires could be used in artificial insemination. This was a turning point. At that time, the AI ​​centers, for the Romagnola breed, had semen stored from over 80 sires, representing a wide range of lines, the blocking of which would have effectively forced the centers to destroy the stored seminal material. This could have caused irreparable damage to the breed and, as a member of the Central Technical Commission, I proposed that a semen bank be set up to recover their germplasm, because this could have been useful for the prophylaxis of any genetic defects and I promised myself to restore their use as soon as I had the opportunity. As a result of this CTC resolution, the number of available sires on AI was drastically reduced to a handful of bulls, several of which would later prove to be carriers of genetic diseases.

The “Ville Unite” herd foundation

Convinced that we could make our contribution to the breed, supporting its development both in Italy and abroad, together with Fred and Gianluca we decided to set up our own herd, to which we added the prefix “Ville Unite”. In September 1990, we purchased a cow named Noemi, by Sole and pregnant to Tarcisio, one of our foundation cows, from the Babini Bros herd in Russi. This cow was followed by others purchased from the herds of Gualtiero Succi, the Batani Bros, Carlo Ravaioli, Giuliano Spazzoli, Primo Neri and Loris Pozzi, as well as the aforementioned Babini Bros. Further subjects were purchased from the Forlì herds of the Fiorentini Bros and the Polgrossi Emilio company, as well as from the herd of Adolfo Pasini in Rimini. These cows all came from deep and consistent families and boasted, in addition to particular morphological correctness, pedigrees representing a wide range of lines. With the idea of ​​submitting our cows to embryo collection, Fred went to the USA to learn the embryo transfer technique and subsequently, after setting up an equipped lab on the farm, we began to superovulate our cows. To ensure the availability of the widest possible range of genetic lines, we proceeded to purchase the semen of the most interesting sires as well as maintaining the semen of the bulls stored by Dr. Guberti at the INFA center in Bologna, which, otherwise, after 1990, would have been destroyed. The fact that three young men in their early twenties were actively dedicating themselves to the Romagnola, carrying out innovative activities, moving independently even on an international level, took the breed environment by surprise, generating amazement and even envy. Our “baptism of the ring” took place at the National Show of Forlì in September 1990, where Gianluca Giuliani, who in the meantime had trained as a handler in the rings in Ireland and Scotland, led Santina, a first calving cow by Marte, to victory in her class. Subsequently, our participation in shows has been numerous and often crowned with success. It can also be said that we have had a significant role in improving the shows organized by Anabic with regard to preparation, grooming and leading the cattle in the ring.

In 1991 Anabic celebrated its 30th anniversary and did so with a major event that saw around 800 head of the 5 Italian beef breeds converge on Bastia Umbra in a September edition of Agriumbria entitled “Giganti Bianchi”. This exhibition, desired by the young Anabic director, Dr. Guido Perosino, and impeccably managed on the field by his staff, coordinated by Lucio Migni, was crowned with great success. On that occasion I acted as a judge in the Romagnola ring alternating with Lucio Migni himself, who had been designated Chief Classifier shortly before. The event, adequately promoted also internationally, attracted several foreign operators to the exhibition and it was at ringside that, together with Fred and Gianluca, we met John Onley, an Australian Agronomist and breeder of the Braford and Romagnola breeds, from Nebo, in central Queensland, who had come to Italy together with some colleagues to visit the Romagnola herds. John and I immediately got on well together and this made the time spent together extremely pleasant, both at the show and during the tour of visits to the herds, carried out in the following days.

John Onley and the Romagnola “down under”

John was an authority in the agronomic and livestock panorama of his Country, in which he had promoted the recovery of some forage sorghum cultivars, as well as creating innovative systems for the containment and handling of livestock and being one of the founders of the Australian Association of Breeders of the Braford breed. What struck me about John was the elegance of his manners, his friendliness, his profound culture and knowledge of livestock but above all his uncommon determination to deepen his knowledge of Romagnola. The breed, which arrived in Australia from New Zealand in the early 1980s, was strongly influenced by the lines of the founder sires introduced in Scotland in the 1970s and by the bulls arriving from Canada dating back to the same period. Australian breeders needed to introduce new bloodlines and John's study was aimed at evaluating which were the most reliable to introduce. During his further visits to Italy I spent time describing to him not only the morphological traits of the breed but also the strong and critical points of the various sirelines, their distinctive traits, the most consistent combinations, suggestions for matings, the most important cow families and their characteristics. John took meticulous note of all this, asking questions and delving into the aspects that most interested him. It should be remembered that in the early 1990s, genome research was in its infancy and it was not yet possible to identify subjects carrying defects as is currently the case. The only weapons available to limit the spread of unwanted genes were a good knowledge of the breed and a solid historical memory. The humility of the approach to the breed, by a great cattleman like him, in addition to the many interesting considerations that emerged during our discussions, were an important enrichment for me. Returning home with clearer ideas on the potential of the breed, John formed a company together with some friends and proceeded in the years between 1992 and 1995, to purchase bulls and heifers for the collection of semen and embryos for Australia. The cattle chosen by John took the road to Denmark with Billund as destination, to the semen and embryo collection center of the Veterinarian Dr. Jorn Erri. The bulls collected were: Adige, Ande, Bulgaro, Cesare, Calore, Caronte, Dingo, Dublino, Ergum and Elisir while among the females there were Avana, Aola, Amona, Bianca, Circe, Diva, Damiana, Diana, Europa. Their genetic heritage has made a valid contribution to the development of the breed in Australia and other Countries and their progeny has established itself in the most prestigious showgrounds on numerous occasions, with positive promotional and commercial repercussions. In 1994 I was invited by the Romagnola Breeders Society of Australia to judge the breed at Beef ’94 in Rockhampton, Queensland. At the important event, which I attended with Fred and Corrado, about a hundred high-level head were on display, making both the classes and the finals extremely competitive. The show was followed by a technical meeting in which I had the opportunity to delve into the judging criteria in a fruitful exchange with the breeders. The event that will remain forever etched in my memory was the standing ovation that the Australian breeders reserved for Corrado, during the closing dinner of the show, for his contribution to the selection of the cattle who had left Italy in the 1970s, laying the foundations for the affirmation of the breed in their Country. On that occasion, Corrado experienced intense emotion for the gratitude and appreciation paid to him by breeders so far from home and at the same time so aware of his abilities. On the sidelines of the exhibition, a tour of the farms was organized, which allowed us to appreciate the good health of the breed in Australia, as well as to see the interesting products born from the embryos produced by our cows. Among these was a very young “Italia Padrone”, a bull who would collect important affirmations in the following years.

My landing in Anabic

In 1993, Anabic had established Italiana Genetica e Servizi for the promotion and marketing of the genetics of Italian breeds in the world and, consequently, the autonomy and resourcefulness of the Ville Unite farm generated distrust and ended up placing us, once again, on the wrong side of the fence. In the same years, the Romagnola herd “La Viola”, owned by Gian Michele Graziani, in Ravenna, was also born, becoming the largest nucleus of the breed as well as a fierce competitor, determined to establish itself on both the domestic and international markets. In September 1994, Anabic organized with great success, at its headquarters, the 1st World Congress of Italian Breeds, which saw the influx of operators from all over the world and for which I took care, together with Lucio Migni, of the selection and grooming of the animals that paraded in an evening event for the congress participants, whom I then accompanied on the post-congress tour of visits to the Romagnola herds. On that same occasion, Anabic laid the foundations for the first export of the breed to South Africa to the “Rosengarten” herd, owned by the entrepreneur Armando Balocco. 1994 also saw the publication, by Anabic, of the brochures relating to the Official Standards of the 5 Italian beef cattle breeds, for which I had drawn the descriptive tables of the different breeds, collaborating, together with Lucio Migni, on the graphic definition of the linear classes and the drafting of the texts. This was the framework when, in May 1995, I was hired by Anabic as head of the Morphological Evaluation Service. A few months later, the director, Dr. Guido Perosino, and the president, Dr. Nicola Marcantonio, left their respective positions and were replaced by the lawyer Giovan Francesco Pugliese, as president, and by Dr. Paolo Canestrari as director. In those years, the Ville Unite herd was quite active in the export of semen, embryos and cattle to various countries and, given that Anabic had its own commercial company with the same ambitions, the management implicitly had a distrustful attitude towards me, to which some breeders from Romagnola also contributed. I must say that this aversion, to which I never got used to and which sometimes brought me to the brink of leaving Anabic, characterised long periods of my career. I alleviated the heaviness I felt by immersing myself in work in search of the satisfactions I needed. But if this attitude allowed me to overcome difficult moments, towards Gianluca Giuliani, owner of the “Ville Unite” herd, the wall of hostility took on the characteristics of a systematic ostracism, which ended up cancelling out any ambition of taking on an active role in the management of the breed. Romagnola was thus deprived of an important opportunity, both in terms of the contribution of ideas and the ability to put them into practice. In May 1997, the Australian Association of Romagnola Breeders and Anabic organized the World Congress of Italian Beef Breeds in Rockhampton. The event saw John Onley at the forefront of its realization and received the appreciation of all the operators present for the impeccable organization and the particularly careful logistics. The Congress was held at the same time as Beef’97, during which both the Romagnola and the Chianina held their respective shows. In particular, the Romagnola entered the ring with a large and very valid team, in which the Ville Unite genetics made the difference starting from the absolute champion of the show, the bull Aldaree Power Plus, by Ande. The return to Italy was marred by the sudden death of Corrado, who left a great void in his family, in me and in those closest to him.

The new millennium begins with BSE

In 2000 the breed, after years of decreasing in numbers, saw its numbers attested rather steadily at 14,000 head. The public contribution to support the breeds in numerical decline had certainly contributed to this result and the commercial situation, although without sensational prices, seemed rather calm. It was the classic calm before the storm that preceded the devastating arrival on the scene of Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE), also known as “Mad Cow Syndrome”. This devastating degenerative disease of the nervous system, caused by a prion transmitted through infected meat meal used as a protein source for cattle feed and transmissible to humans, had enormous media coverage, shaking up markets throughout Europe and causing a drastic collapse in beef consumption. These were difficult times and many months passed before any signs of recovery were noticeable.

Fortunately, the native Italian breeds, whose meat could boast the PGI mark recognized by the EEC and managed by the Consortium for the Protection of “Vitellone Bianco dell’Appennino Centrale” since 1998, were the only ones to be included in a fully traceable supply chain. The obligations established by the PGI protocol, relating to livestock feeding, regulated the use of fodder and silage, promoting the use of farm products and prohibiting the use of by-products and animal meal, aiming for high quality meat and consumer protection. In the difficult market conditions that had arisen, this attracted the interest of large-scale distribution on white breeds, resulting in a rush to purchase that allowed their breeders to be the first to overcome the crisis following the advent of BSE. The favorable market conditions restored confidence in breeders and saw the Romagnola breed, after many years, increase its numbers, which in 2005 stood at 16,700 heads distributed across 568 farms. In 2005, Anabic was involved in the organization of the World Congress of Italian Beef Cattle Breeds, held in Gubbio in May, which attracted operators from all over the world to the event and which was crowned with great success.

The final parade of the champions of the Italian breeds, held at night at Villa Benveduti, represented the culmination of a great effort that left an indelible memory in all the figures involved. Lucio Migni also contributed significantly to its realization, actively engaged in the field during the entire event despite having been tenaciously fighting for several years against a lymphoma that would have given him no escape. His death, which occurred in March 2006, at only 42 years of age, on the eve of the Agriumbria, where the Chianina would have held its National show, transformed the event into a heartfelt and choral tribute to him as a man and technician to whom the Anabic Genetic Center of S. Martino in Colle was later named in 2009. With him, a point of reference for the selection of Italian breeds and the Chianina in particular has passed away, as well as a dear friend with particular charisma and uncommon human qualities. Only a few weeks later, John Onley, a gentleman in his ways and a prominent figure in the international environment of the Romagnola breed, whose contribution was fundamental to the development of the breed in Australia and to whom I was linked by a sincere friendship, also suddenly passed away. These enormous losses left a huge void, transforming 2006 into a year to forget. In 2007, during the presidency of Fausto Luchetti, Dr. Paolo Canestrari left the management of Anabic and Dr. Roberta Guarcini became the new director. Among the notable events held during her leadership, the international Congress, entitled “On the Trail of the Podolians”, held at the Mediateca, in Matera on July 2009 and dedicated to the European Grey breeds, had a prominent place. It was attended by technicians and university professors from the Countries that are custodians grey breeds of Podolian origin, such as Ukraine, Hungary, Serbia, Croatia, Greece and Turkey, as well as professors from various Italian universities and representatives of the institutional world. The scientific sessions, held in Matera, were followed by a tour of visits to the Podolica breed herds in Puglia, Basilicata and Calabria as well as to the Bulls Selection Centre in Laurenzana, PZ. Another important event also coincided with the celebration of the 50th anniversary of Anabic, held in conjunction with the 2011 edition of Agriumbria Show, in Bastia Umbra.

The end of a System

In the meantime, the national livestock system was experiencing a phase of upheaval and radical restructuring, in a context made particularly precarious by the uncertainty about funding for selection and the need to contain its costs. The ministerial cuts to funding led the National Breed Associations to optimize the increasingly limited resources available by sometimes reducing their staff, resorting to social safety nets and going into survival mode. Meanwhile, the peripheral system saw the Provincial and Regional Breeders' Associations in great difficulty, leading AIA (Italian Breeders' Association) to modify its Statute to redefine the general operational scheme and give continuity to functional controls. The upheaval that characterized this phase not only saw the disappearance of the Provincial Breeders' Associations, which merged into their regional counterparts (ARA), but was also characterized by the spread of professional organizations in the livestock system, outlining scenarios that until a few years earlier no one would have imagined. In the meantime, the EU funds provided by the PSRN through the I-BEEF and I-BEEF2 projects for the period between 2014 and 2023, have stabilized the economic framework, allowing the National Breed Associations to continue to carry out their activities.

Since the advent of the new millennium, the Romagnola breed had maintained its workforce almost unchanged until, around 2010, the long post-BSE wave exhausted its effects. The questionable marketing management implemented by the IGP Protection Consortium, which could have diversified the offer in the phase in which the white breeds were at the center of attention, ended up channeling the entire production towards large-scale distribution which, once the phase of necessity was over, inevitably imposed its own rules. The interest of the large-scale distribution therefore focused on the Chianina, which thanks to its aura of "Tuscanness" was the best known to the general public and therefore the most saleable. The Protection Consortium has supported this orientation by privileging the Chianina and largely disregarding its own mission of protecting other breeds in their respective territories. This has put the Marchigiana and especially the Romagnola in difficulty, which despite having all the requirements of a competitive meat breed, lacks alternative structures to the large-scale retail trade in its area, and for which the marketing strategies should have been reviewed. The resulting commercial difficulties have ended up accelerating the decrease in the breed's numbers, which in 2022 were reduced to only 10,000 overall units distributed across 300 herds, and with a further decreasing trend. We have thus reached the epilogue of my involvement with an official role in the selective system of Italian breeds, given that the end of 2023 coincided with my retirement. It was a long period of time lived intensely, which allowed me to evaluate throughout Italy and to judge on numerous occasions in shows of all levels throughout the country, as well as abroad in about fifteen events of the various Italian breeds held in various Countries.

A personal tribute to the breed

Throughout my professional life, I have been asked several times if I had ever had the idea of ​​collecting my experiences with the Romagnola breed in a book, so that I could share its historical memory. I have always been convinced that the most appropriate way for a seedstock breeder to demonstrate his skills is to let the facts speak for themselves. I would therefore have preferred to leave my mark on the breed by building quality livestock, but the drastic decline in numbers, which has characterized the recent history of Romagnola, made me realize that I would not have had the time. So I thought of giving shape to a personal tribute to the breed, which would retrace the most significant part of its epic, passing through the breeders who have marked it. Of the eras that I could have taken into consideration, the 20th century was undoubtedly the most significant, both for the exceptional events that characterized it and for the parable that the Romagnola described in the same period of time, going from the Parisian triumphs at the beginning of the century to the institution of the Herd Book, to the boom in stocks and the risk of extinction at the dawn of the new millennium. I therefore chose to trace, through a site developed ad hoc, a path through images in which the protagonists were the most important sires and in which the historical references were simple "brush strokes" useful for placing them in time. Considering the conspicuous amount of material preserved over the years, I could have simply used the photographs in my possession for this purpose. This would have undeniably played an important role from a documentary perspective but would have made this work colder and more impersonal. So, starting from 1989, I began to draw the bulls, portraying them as faithfully as possible, starting from photographs of the most varied extraction and archiving the drawings, which over time have become a thousand, ordering them by sire lines. The sources I have drawn from have been countless: books, show catalogues, publications of the Provincial Agricultural Inspectorates, promotional brochures of bull stations and AI centres, private archives of friends, breeders, bull station owners and livestock traders, archives of Anabic and of the APA of the breeding area, as well as the internet and social media. The registry and biographical references relating to the various sires have not always been easy to find and the numerous homonyms, the occasional transcription errors of the hand-written registration numbers and some typos have sometimes complicated the picture. I thought of including some photos so that the faithfulness of the drawings can be assessed with respect to the reference source. For each line, a summary diagram and a summary of its history, of the owners who favored its development, of the historical period and of the area in which each line developed have been drawn up, in addition, when possible, to weight records and the most striking exhibition results obtained.

I hope that the web site can help those who are approaching the Romagnola breed to appreciate it more fully, given that the figures who have personally experienced its golden age are increasingly fewer and that even the related documentary material is becoming increasingly difficult to find.

Today I see the countryside of the Romagna plain and the stables, once teeming with life, inexorably empty or destined for other uses. I think of the new generations, for whom the bovine and its rhythms are unknown and absolutely dissonant compared to today's world. It is something unimaginable for those who have not lived them, which harks back to relatively recent but now very distant times, and I find it disconcerting the speed with which culture, history and traditions are forgotten even in the territory that saw them flourish. I think of the skills, sensitivity, common sense and ambition with which generations of breeders, with few means available, have been able to build so much beauty. I hope, however, that databases, the progress of reproductive techniques, genomics and increasingly advanced technological means can in the future – perhaps with the help of those foreign countries where the Romagnola has found refuge and flourished – give new strength to this wonderful breed or at least help us to keep it rooted in its lands of origin. But I will return to this point at the end of this book, in which I will try to describe what the breeding of the Romagnola cattle breed has been and what it has meant in our countryside, for our farmers.

ORIGINS AND DIFFUSION

The history of the Romagnola breed has the characteristics of an epic that has seen the breed itself at the center of a slow evolution and epochal events. Its origins date back to the Bos Primigenius or European Auroch, a large wild bovine with long horns depicted in various sites since the Neolithic, also described by Julius Caesar in De Bello Gallico and extinct in 1627 when the last specimen, a female, died in the Jactorow forest, in Poland. The European Grey Breeds would derive from a subspecies of the Bos Primigenius, the Bos Primigenius Podolicus. These cattle would have reached Italy in the 4th century AD. following the invasion of the Goths led by Agilulf, finding in the eastern part of the Po Valley south of the Po River and corresponding to the current provinces of Bologna, Ferrara, Forlì-Cesena, Ravenna and Rimini, the breeding area where the Romagnola breed originated. It cannot be ruled out that local aurochs may have also contributed to the origin of the breed. Long-horned cattle are in fact described by Virgil, just as, going back in time, the influences of Middle Eastern cattle on the genome of some Italian grey breeds are certain, in particular for the Podolica breed. Such influence on the bovine populations of the Mediterranean area is not surprising, considering the imprimatur of the "fertile crescent" regarding the cultivation of cereals and the domestication of livestock. No less important was the contribution of the Phoenicians and their colonies for the dissemination of these techniques. The Greeks also later gave their contribution. In fact, the term “italos” is Greek, meaning “bull” and by describing our peninsula as the “Land of Cattle”, it actually gave it its name. Even in the Byzantine mosaics of the Basilica of San Vitale, in Ravenna, dating back to the 6th century, the image of a grey bull represents the evangelist Luke, which, due to the slight hump on the withers and the long tail, recalls a Taurus-Indic bovine, probably reflecting the artist’s familiarity with this type of cattle. Among the native Italian beef cattle breeds, the one least influenced by the grey cattle of Podolian stock is certainly the Chianina, which boasts Etruscan origins and was described with characteristics very similar to those of today already in Roman times. The subsequent barbarian invasions therefore marked an epochal turning point not only for the history of the Nation but also for the development of the bovine ethnic groups that would have ensued. The Romagnola cattle breed is ascribed to the group of European Grey Breeds of Podolian origin. Podolia is the region of Ukraine from which a series of similar breeds radiated to Eastern Europe, Turkey, Greece, the Balkans, Istria and Italy, sharing a grey coat, black skin pigmentation, well-developed horns, lyre-shaped in cows and half moon-shaped in bulls, and the fact that calves are born wheaten in colour and change the colour of their coat, gradually becoming white around three months of age. The group of grey breeds includes the following ethnic groups:

- Ukrainian Grey (Ukraine);

- Sura de Stepa (Romania);

- Hungarian Grey (Hungary)

- Iskar (Bulgaria);

- Boz Irk (Turkey);

- Sykia and Katerini (Greece);

- Mursi (Albania);

- Boskarin (Montenegro);

- Podolsko Govece (Serbia);

- Slavonski Podolac (Croatia)

- Istarsko Govedo (Istria)

These breeds are today, in some cases, extinct or reduced to a minimum, while others are the object of recovery programs and are seeing their numbers recover, as in the case of the Hungarian Grey, the Boz Irk and the Istrian. The Pugliese del Veneto, now unfortunately extinct, also descended from this last breed, whose breeding area mainly included the provinces of Rovigo, Venice and Padua as well as the Emilian provinces of Ferrara and part of the province of Bologna. Despite this, among the countries in which the grey breeds have found their breeding cradles, Italy is the one that has preserved them in greater numbers. The five Italian breeds protected by Anabic, Marchigiana, Chianina, Romagnola, Maremmana and Podolica, consist of a total heritage of about 150,000 head and can take advantage of a structured selection program whose support offers them a greater possibility of being passed down to future generations.

Historical notes

But returning to the Romagnola and its history, once settled in the eastern part of the Po Valley, south of the Po River, in what would become the cradle of the breed's origin, the grey cattle came into contact with local ethnic groups, not of Podolica origin, with short horns, similar to the current Reggiana and Bianca Valpadana breeds. This would also be confirmed by the presence, in the Bologna area, of the so-called "Bazzana variety", with a more or less dark wheaten coat and scarcely pigmented, documented up to the 18th century. Even the dialect names "Ro" and "Bunin" and their variants, relating to the oxen yoked to the right and left of the tiller of agricultural vehicles, cited by numerous bibliographic sources, would derive from the terms Rubrum and Bonellum, to indicate respectively, as reported by contracts registered since the 14th century, a subject with a tawny coat and the other with a grey coat.

For centuries, in the hilly area and also in the coastal strip of Romagna, the large estate dominated and the livestock was raised in the wild. The progressive spread of the sharecropping contract, replacing the previous forms of land concession, led to the organization of the estate intended as a farm unit, on which the farmhouse was built. Together with the cultivated land of the estates, the manor houses also contributed to delineating the landscape, usually surrounded by small woods, in which the owner did not stay habitually, going there for periods of vacation and to periodically check his properties. With the advent of Napoleon and the inclusion of Romagna in the Cisalpine Republic, in 1789, the fiefs were abolished, the number of convents was reduced, the privileges of the ecclesiastics and all their tax exemptions were eliminated. A network of bureaucratic structures for the various sectors of the economy was also established. The lands expropriated from the Church were sold at auction to private individuals, or entrusted to Municipal Communities or placed to endow Hospitals. The sale of ecclesiastical assets, however, benefited mostly the former nobility and the wealthy bourgeoisie, also thanks to incentives that allowed the purchase of land at a low price and payment deferrals, while no agrarian reform was implemented to benefit small property. Even the use of free grazing was regulated through the payment of a tax per head. The benefits received by the nobles were maintained even later and led to the search for greater productivity of their properties. Free-range breeding progressively decreased while the landed properties were organized into colonies, each with its own stable, equipped with one or more bull-stations.

An “all-rounder breed”

The stables, built with great care, often spacious and well-lit, were sometimes true works of art, with vaults and columns to delimit the stalls. Cattle continued to assist humans in carrying out agricultural work, developing the typology indicative of the predominantly dynamic attitude that they had to perform. Furthermore, in the context of an agriculture based on traditional crop rotation and self-sustenance, fresh cows were milked to provide milk and cheese, male calves in excess of the farm's needs were sold, while meat production, which had long been marginal, was mainly obtained by animals at the end of their career. Cattle also produced manure, used as a soil improver, and provided warmth to the peasant family during the winter months. Due to their essential role, cattle were carefully cared for by the herdsmen, watered twice a day and regularly groomed, developing a constant relationship with humans. Calves destined to become oxen were castrated within six months of age, or at most around one year.

The oxen were also regularly shod and, having to work in pairs, were chosen from a young age looking for a marked mutual resemblance, as well as the necessary structural soundness. The horns were also important, providing a grip for anchoring the animals to the yoke and the agricultural vehicle, and already in calves they were the object of attention so that they assumed the right direction and the desired symmetry. At fairs and markets the cattle were then frequently adorned with bands, bows and wool tassels, generally red in colour, originally linked to popular superstition. Also frequently used were blankets for the cattle, usually made of linen or home-woven hemp, often rust-printed and bearing the image of St. Anthony the Abbot. Their purpose was to protect the sweaty cattle at the end of an intense effort or to serve as decoration on the occasion of fairs or parades. The Napoleonic reforms also left their mark on the bands of livestock, which were often decorated with white, red and blue tricolour pennants, as a sign of the landowners' deference to the French general.

The impact of the industrial revolution

However, it was not only Napoleon's approach that marked the history of Romagnola because another strong wave of innovation, starting from Great Britain between 1780 and 1830, the industrial revolution, would make its effects felt on agriculture and livestock technologies not only in Europe but throughout the world. Initially characterised by the discovery of the steam engine and its use on an industrial scale, this revolution was also supported by laws that favoured the wealthier classes and large landowners, enabling them to invest huge amounts of capital in this challenge and attracting large masses of workers to industrial cities. The increase in production and population that followed had important consequences on agriculture and livestock farming, improving productivity and increasing the availability of food capable of satisfying a market made more lively by growing well-being. All domestic species of zootechnical interest were affected by a change that required them to be transformed into more efficient production units. It was far-sighted and capable English zootechnicians, such as Robert Bakewell and the brothers Charles and Robert Collins, who, around 1850, gave life to the first specialized bovine breeds for meat production, such as the Hereford and the Shorthorn. The initial selective phase, characterized by inbreeding matings to fix the desired characteristics, was supported by periodic weight checks as well as by an innovative and fundamental element: the Herd Book. These breeds thus quickly saw their notoriety expand and crossed the borders of Great Britain to land in Europe, the United States, Australia and numerous other countries, earning a solid reputation as cosmopolitan breeds and contributing to the creation of new breeds. This innovative wave also reached Italy, prompting the most fertile and open minds in the agricultural world to seek solutions that would lead to qualitative and quantitative improvements in agricultural and livestock production and to a higher income for the operators involved.

The work of Engineer Leopoldo Tosi

Among these figures, Leopoldo Tosi (1847 -1917), originally from Rimini, assumed particular importance. After graduating in engineering from the Royal Technical Institute of Milan, now the Polytechnic, in 1876 he joined his father-in-law Ercole Ruffi in the administration of the Tenuta dei Principi Torlonia in S. Mauro di Romagna, now S. Mauro Pascoli, a large landed property of 1,940 hectares, located between Cesena and Rimini, later renting it in 1885. Giovanni Pascoli (1855 -1912), a student of Carducci and the greatest Italian decadent poet, was also born at the Tenuta Torlonia, the central nucleus of which was known by all as “La Torre”. His father Ruggero, administrator of the estate itself, was assassinated in 1867, while returning home in a carriage from Cesena, where he was supposed to meet an emissary of the Torlonias. The murder, the reasons for which were never clarified, had a devastating effect on the Pascoli family and Giovanni, 11 years old at the time, was forever affected by it, as is evident from the many references to the event in his poetic production. The friendship between the poet and Leopoldo Tosi bound them for life and is documented by an extensive correspondence. Tosi's action at Tenuta Torlonia resulted in significant changes that ranged from the improvement of agronomic techniques, to the introduction of tobacco cultivation, silkworm breeding, the expansion of the areas cultivated with vineyards and the production of wines, aided in this last activity by his son-in-law Giovanni Briolini, a chemist and oenologist. But if the innovative process from an agronomic point of view was rather fast, that of the livestock heritage occurred more slowly. When Tosi arrived at La Torre, the estate had 200 colonies with 500 head of cattle and two bulls worked in his stud: Vernocchi, bought in Romagna, and Volente, a Chianina x Podolian cross purchased in the Marche region. The cattle in the farmers' stables were of poor quality, incorrect, narrow in transverse diameters, with narrow chests, tight ribs, sloping rumps, poor muscle mass and low food conversion capacity. Determined to change this status and to transform the cattle into a source of income, Tosi eliminated the functioning sires and proceeded to purchase, on the various markets of Romagna, the subjects he considered most suitable for his purposes. His collaborators Bigi Nanni and Luigi Bilancioni helped him in this endeavor, and they were later joined by his son-in-law, Prof. Dino Sbrozzi. The purchased new sires were concentrated at the Boaria Centrale, where an average of seven bulls worked. In those years, important reclamation and water management works had been started in Romagna, and agriculture was characterized by a rapid evolution of cultivation techniques. The type of livestock that Tosi intended to build would have to accommodate these changes and if maintaining the dynamic attitude was necessary, the search for a greater aptitude for meat production was equally necessary, because it would have increased the income obtained both from the sale of young excess livestock and from that at the end of its career. The improvement of agricultural techniques would have guaranteed more abundant harvests, allowing a qualitative and quantitative increase in the rations administered to the livestock, which would have gained in terms of efficiency, anticipating the age of commercial maturity. The cornerstones on which Tosi's vision took shape were different. A typicality had to be defined that identified the breed, starting from the color of the coat, the shape of the head and the horns. The accentuated skin and apical pigmentation, the elasticity and abundance of the skin, the presence and development of the dewlap, traits linked to the physiology of thermoregulation, had to accommodate the animals' resistance to fatigue, to which agricultural work would have subjected them. The necessary structural functionality required particular attention to the correctness of the limbs and feet, as well as the fluidity of the gait. With regard to the capacity for growth, its increase required an increase in the transverse diameters of the chest, with a more arched rib cage and a greater ingestion capacity. The typical truncated cone silhouette with an anterior base, typical of working breeds, had to evolve by increasing the volumes of the intermediate and posterior parts of the trunk, which would become longer, assuming a more cylindrical shape. Finally, the aptitude for meat production, which should have assumed an equal role with respect to the dynamic one, had to be pursued through greater muscle coverage, in particular at the level of the dorsal-lumbar area and the hindquarters. There was a further trait that Tosi intended to pursue: the balance of the forms, which would have given the cattle an added value on the seedstock cattle market. In addition to basing the selection on these criteria, pursuing it with strict formal rigor, Leopoldo Tosi established the stud genealogical book, which he called Herd Book, diligently documented the events, measurements and systematic weight controls, determined the composition and quantity of the rations administered and calculated the food conversion ratio for the growing subjects. With regard to the productivity of the cows, the calving intervals were considered while their maternal capacity was assessed through the monthly weighing of the nursing calves.

The successes in Paris

All this preceded by half a century the start of the official selection, which would only be started in 1930, and determined the achievement of the earliest recognitions. Already in the last years of the 1800s the cattle of the Torlonia Estate obtained significant affirmations in numerous exhibitions held in Romagna, being presented with success also at the Shows of Turin and Milan. The foundation sires of the nucleus formed by Tosi were: Vivante, Dmangon and Primo. From this last sire descends Ceccone, the symbolic bull of the team presented in Paris in 1900, which sanctioned the affirmation of the Romagnola breed also on an international level. The group of 20 head from the Tenuta Torlonia presented at the World Exhibition in Paris had been chosen by Tosi with extreme care, aiming both at the correctness of the individuals and at their general uniformity. In addition to Ceccone, the bull Attila was also part of it, while among the cows were Bella and Flora, two of the best cows of the estate. The cattle obtained important individual and group recognitions, competing with foreign breeds and in particular with the British Hereford, whose team was particularly aggressive. To complete this triumph, Leopoldo Tosi was named Knight of the Order of Agricultural Merit by the French Minister of Agriculture Jean Dupuy. The successes achieved in Paris had a wide echo in the specialized press both in Italy and abroad and earned Tosi numerous awards. For the Torlonia estate the commercial impact on the sale of breeding stock was enormous, so much so that if before the “World Expo” in Paris the bulls sold annually were around a hundred, in the years immediately following over 200 were sold to buyers not only from Romagna, but from the entire national territory. The search for morphological correctness and harmony, which Tosi had pursued from the beginning, now bore striking fruit. Some subjects were also sold abroad, in France, Germany, Great Britain, Hungary, Romania and Russia. In the early 1900s a bull was sent as a gift to Tsar Nicholas II. Also from Russia was Count Erast Konstantinovich Brodskij, a breeder of Ukrainian Grey cattle and a regular customer of Tenuta Torlonia who, in addition to the bull Primo, also purchased the famous Ceccone, of whom all trace was lost following the October Revolution. Despite the wide consensus obtained, Tosi did not rest on his laurels and returned from Paris determined to correct the traits of his cattle that he considered limiting. Some of his considerations, reported by his son-in-law, Prof. Dino Sbrozzi, are particularly indicative. According to Tosi, the Romagnola breed should have improved the strength of the topline, the set of the rump and the correctness of the tail head. The dimensions, linked to the growth potential, should have been maintained, while the muscularity at the loins, at the rump, and particularly at the thigh and buttock, not sufficiently descended and convex, should have been increased. Regarding the proportions of the trunk, which he wanted to be deep and roomy, Tosi believed that its closeness to the ground should not be determined by the excessive shortness of the limbs. Unlike the British Hereford, created as a specialized beef breed in a country where horses were used to do the agricultural work, the Romagnola, in addition to producing meat, also had to be used to pull agricultural machinery and, above all, to plough the often clayey and tenacious soil, which required strong, functional and not too short limbs. This intelligent, visionary and capable man had shaped the modern Romagnola cattle, starting from an ordinary material and transforming it into an efficient, profitable means of production, suited to the agronomic evolution of the territory. At his death in 1917, the Tenuta dei Principi Torlonia was a modern and efficient entity, with 150 colonies and 1,500 head of cattle.

Medoro as Ribot

Although the dynamic aptitude was still required, Tosi had laid the foundations for the evolution of the model towards a mono-aptitude specialization typology for the production of meat, which would characterise the Romagnola breed in the following decades. As happened to Federico Tesio for the famous Ribot, not even Leopoldo Tosi managed to see his masterpiece, Medoro, the undisputed founder of the breed, whose lineage continues to spread even today, and other lines, among the most valid of the current Romagnola, also come from sires born at “ LaTorre”. To do justice to the complexity of Tosi's figure, however, it must be underlined how he dedicated himself to the various activities in which he was involved with the same intensity shown towards zootechnics, starting from agronomy, entomology and oenology, passing through architecture, literature and philanthropy. All these traits were explored in depth during a celebratory event held at the Torre di S. Mauro Pascoli on 18 November 2017, on the centenary of his death. The initiative, sponsored by the Municipality of S. Mauro and the Casa Pascoli Museum, was organized by Dr. Luca Barducci, a fellow veterinarian as well as a passionate historian, in the presence of the Palloni and Briolini families, descendants of Leopoldo Tosi. The interesting presentations that were the subject of the seminar were held by agronomists, entomologists, architects, men of letters and historians. I was granted the privilege of speaking about the Romagnola breed, in relation to which, after having traced its origins and history, I focused on its evolutionary path following the work of Tosi. I remember that someone commented: - It seems like the script of a movie ... -.

A saga between glory and tragedy

This "movie", based on a thousand-year-old history, has been marked both by moments of glory and by immense tragedies. Its protagonists, sometimes famous and enlightened and more often anonymous and silent, have given life to a "zootechnical marvel" that, in addition to contributing to the development of its territory of origin, has been able to establish itself on an international level. The breeders, sharecroppers, factors, and stud farm managers were joined by middlemen, merchants, blacksmiths, veterinarians and many other figures, such as carters, carpenters, blacksmiths and others, who could be defined as the “induced” sector of the Romagnola breed. For centuries, the relationship between man and his livestock seemed unchangeable, or characterized by little change. Cattle supported man's hard work in the fields and, being indispensable, were generally treated with consideration. In addition to being a driving force, they also represented capital that could be drawn upon in times of need. The stable was an integral part of peasant life and came to life when the animals needed to be watered and fed, sometimes late at night, before plowing, continuing to mark the life of the family even in the evening, especially in winter, when it became the warmest place in the house and hosted women's work, children's games and sleep, wakes and threshing. If for some, cattle were a necessary evil, a burden that was tolerated only out of necessity, for others they represented a passion, something beautiful to show off and be proud of. Until the industrial revolution and other important historical events shuffled the cards, this state of affairs seemed suspended in time for a while, giving the illusory impression of resisting the impact of progress. The arrival of Napoleon in Romagna, the redistribution of land expropriated from the Church, land reclamation and the improvement of agricultural techniques created the conditions favorable to a change that Tosi managed to ride, transforming livestock into an important economic resource, which would be able to withstand the devastating impact of two world wars.

The Official Herd Book

Between the first and second world wars, when the breed boasted a staff of about 530,000 heads, the Official Herd Book was established. An essential tool for any genetic improvement program, the Register, created under the aegis of the Ministry of Agriculture and managed locally by the Provincial Itinerant Chairs, marked the beginning of cattle registration of and the start of weight checks as well as the collection of production data. Registered animals were tattooed on the left ear with the initials of their province and a sequential number. The first animal to be registered in the province of Ravenna was the bull Medoro, considered the founder of the breed, who was tattooed with the 1/RA. In subsequent years, with the identification of the "core bulls", the marking criteria were modified, tattooing registered animals with an identifying initials for each sire and a sequential number. The initials identifying Inverno's offspring, for example, were INVE, while for Trento's offspring it was TR, for Mistero's it was MST, for Baluardo's it was AAD, etc. Even the name of each individual, currently assigned upon registration with an initial that, since 1991, has followed alphabetical order, has undergone some changes over time. Initially, naming was optional for both males and females. Furthermore, for males, it was often the stud farm owners who gave them their names, which, in fact, in older show catalogs, did not appear before 24 months of age.In the early years of the second post-war period, the Romagnola breed restored its numbers, halved following the heavy raids carried out by the retreating German army, experiencing, despite the enormous wounds left by the conflict, a favorable period, dictated both by the needs related to agricultural work and by the desire for redemption of the tenacious people of Romagna. The self-esteem of the Romagna farmers is proverbial and is evident in the care with which the land is maintained, from the roses planted at the head of the orchards, from the order that dominates the landscape. The same ambition was directed towards the livestock and materialized in the effort to produce quality subjects by resorting to the best sires. In the stables of the plain, in particular, the livestock was fed with care, resting on abundant bedding and being regularly groomed. To prevent the animals from wearing out their horns by rubbing them against the walls, the walls were often covered in wood. The smaller calves were left free to roam in the farmyard, or confined in special pens for a large part of the day, for adequate functional exercise.

Attention to detail

The containment means training began early, gradually accustoming the young stock to the nibble. Even the horns were the object of particular attention and, if they took on unwanted directions, especially in males, use was made of tie rods and correctors of various type, to give them the correct shape. These operations had to be carried out gradually, alternating them with rest periods, to prevent the horn case, subjected to excessive stress, from forming cracks or even breaking. The horns were greased quite regularly and always before fairs or shows. Similar attention was also reserved for adult animals, correcting any asymmetries with various techniques, which included sticking the horn into freshly baked bread to soften it, and then applying traction to direct it correctly. In the event of accidental breakage of a horn, if the stump was long enough to allow it, the blemish was remedied by adapting the horn case of a slaughtered animal to it, fixing it with mastic and filing it carefully. The heavy horns were thinned with a rasp, and then smoothed using glass shards. Traders were particularly skilled in tampering with horns, often with the aim of making subjects appear younger whose declared age did not correspond to their real age. For adult males, the walls of the stalls, especially in the stud farms, were covered in wood to prevent the bulls from wearing out their horns due to repeated rubbing, which constitutes an attitude of dominance. During shows, if the bulls' horns were worn, metal shells were applied to replicate their shape, giving them a more pointed and elegant appearance. At the same time as these interventions, the necessary periodic farriery operations were also carried out, consisting of the functional trimming of the hooves and shoeing, applied in particular to oxen. Shoeing could also be corrective, to attenuate postural defects or defects in the direction of the feet and consisted of the temporary application, on young subjects, of thicknesses capable of modifying the supports and gradually correcting the leg set. Skin pigmentation and the coat were also the object of care and attention. When cattle were still used for agricultural work, a certain rusticity in the animals was desirable. To make a light coat darker, the subject was wet and then kept in the sun. Prolonged exposure to solar radiation was also useful for intensifying the pigment, especially in subjects kept in stables during the winter months. To make a dark coat lighter, the animal was instead covered in chalk, flour or talcum powder and wiped with a cloth. The fur of young cattle, longer and woollier than that of adult subjects, could also be ruffled and fixed with laundry soap to attenuate certain defects, or to give greater convexity, for example, to the profile of the hindquarters. With regard to the structure of the animals, the measures used, especially by traders, were so many and not all legal that they cannot be described in a few lines. The bulls for sale were shown to the buyer in the best possible light and were sometimes presented free in a box in which a surface of bundles of wood had been prepared and covered with abundant litter.

This sort of elastic carpet made the movement of the animals particularly elegant and helped to attenuate any structural defects. Some unscrupulous sellers would even stick a pin in the umbilical skin fold of a bull with a loose top line, which was corrected by the resulting pain-relieving reaction. Other illicit tampering involved the alteration of the ear tattoo, with the aim of falsifying the identity of the animal.

Nutritionists before their times

Another aspect that is worth dwelling on is related to the feeding of the cattle. In the lowland farm, crop rotation usually made available the straw, grass, hay and flour necessary for most of the cattle needs. On the hilly area, as is still the case today, semi-wild seasonal grazing was widespread, on natural polyphyte meadows, for the period between spring and late autumn. The number of annual cuts varied depending on the altitude, the composition of the soil and rainfall, from one in the mountain areas to at least three and up to six in the plains. The first cut of alfalfa was the most essential because it arrived in a period of the year in which supplies were running out. Furthermore, being rich in grasses, it was particularly appetizing for the livestock and its administration was more abundant, while the second and third cuts, with higher protein content, were administered to supplement the ration. In some areas, to save forage, hay was mixed with straw, chopping both. Green alfalfa was always administered when the cattle had been hayed, to avoid the risk of flatulence. Other products, such as sugar beets and apples, were preserved for the winter season, grated and administered by mixing them with flours. Beet pulp and collars were ensiled in special pits and used as food during the winter. None of the resources offered by the farm were wasted. Even the leaves of the elm trees, which served as living support in the rows of vines, were collected and administered to the cattle, as well as the mowing of the ditches. Dry foliage, straw, husks and corn stalks could be used as bedding. Among the protein sources used in the ration was often the fava bean, usually soaked and then administered together with the flours. The list of the latter is quite long and, in addition to corn flour, barley flour, and bran, various types of middlings and by-products were administered, based on their affordability and availability in the different areas. The flours were administered both dry and moistened in the form of mash. The ration of young seedstock cattle was particularly careful. The vegetative tips of the wheat and sometimes eggs were added to the mash and even boiled flax seeds, used as a refresher, were mixed with the flours. In the stud farms it was also quite common to administer previously moistened oats to the bulls, which had been allowed to germinate and added to their mash. Bulls were usually kept in tone, in an intermediate body condition, without weighing them down too much, to avoid excessive weight gain on the hind limbs during the rearing. It was also widely believed that too much feeding made bulls more lively and aggressive, increasing the risk of accidents, which were not uncommon, for those who had to look after them. If the bulls had to be prepared for shows, the energy component of the ration was gradually increased. If the rations were changed too suddenly and the flours administered in excessive quantities, the accumulation of catabolites could determine the onset of skin rashes, which were usually soothed with ointments based on lard and flower of sulphur. If the excess food was prolonged over time, the consequences could leave permanent signs especially in young subjects, in which the overload of the skeletal structure, still growing and not completely calcified, could determine the alteration of the leg set, which, initially affecting the forelimbs, could subsequently, as a consequence of postural changes, also characterize the hind legs.

Once the exhibition events were concluded, a less intense diet was returned to and integrated with refreshing preparations such as the aforementioned flaxseed decoction and sometimes also with milk. The bullcalves, once weaned, were subjected to a diet that guaranteed adequate growth and harmonious development, usually avoiding the administration of excessively intense rations and ensuring that, in the event of sale, the subjects quickly got used to the dietary change they would have to face. Some practices, attributable to religious and popular tradition, also included the administration of blessed bread to the livestock on the occasion of the feast of St. Anthony the Abbot, protector of herds, whose effigy was omnipresent in the stables. Other customs, not uniformly respected, included the distribution of more abundant rations on the occasion of certain religious holidays, such as, for example, the Epiphany, as a thank you for their patient work. It was not uncommon for animals, usually tied to the post, to get carpal hygromas, hitting their knees against the manger, especially during feeding. In this case, the area was massaged daily with homemade blistering ointments, based on lard and iodine tincture. It should be emphasized that for a long period of time, before the appearance of antibiotics and ready-to-use pharmaceutical products, extensive use was made of the Galenic preparations of the traditional pharmacopoeia as well as countless homemade infusions and medications used on livestock as needed. The knowledge that farmers of the past had regarding the different plant essences, their properties and methods of administration was remarkable and deserves a separate treatise.

Training for the yoke

A mention should also be made of the techniques used in taming working livestock, an aspect that required time and patience and that did not only concern oxen, but also cows and heifers. The animals had to be trained gradually, first accustoming them to being tied and led in pairs, then being yoked without any towing and subsequently subjected to pulling increasingly heavier vehicles. Each animal was yoked, from the beginning, always on the same side of the drawbar. In the drawbars, the oxen always formed the pair closest to the agricultural vehicle, bearing the greatest strain, especially during ploughing. The drawbars applied to the plough could be formed by a variable number of pairs of animals, depending on the desired depth for the digging. Usually two “professional” cows were yoked at the head, while the heifers, more lively and often intemperate, were always yoked in the intermediate positions, to force them to stay “in ranks”. The cattle were subjected to work during the coolest hours of the day and brought back to the stable during the warmest hours, while the cows in advanced pregnancy were used only for the lightest work and were kept at rest for at least twenty days after calving. In the plains, in addition to ploughs, cattle pulled wheeled vehicles, such as carts and farm wagons, while in the hills and mountains sleds were commonly used. The “caveja” was inserted into the tiller of the farm wagon, or plaustro, and is considered the symbol of Romagna. It was made up of a wrought iron rod ending at the top in a plate decorated with rings and allegorical images. The corresponding term, in Italian, is "cavicchia", referring to its shape and its purpose was to prevent the tiller from slipping forward when the ground was downhill. The rings jingled when the vehicle was in motion and the sound warned passers-by of the transit of the wagon. Animal pulling required a specific technique, in addition to the use of a dense series of gestures, tools, ropes and pegs, the terminology of which, once in common use in the Romagna dialect, is now obsolete or completely disappeared.

The contract with an handshake

Many of the commercial customs related to livestock also suffered the same fate. The sales contract, traditionally sanctioned by a handshake between seller and buyer in the presence of a witness, usually the broker, had the validity of a written contract. The clauses of the contract itself could be variable and provided for payment at the time of sale only for slaughter cattle, while for seedstock and working cattle, payment was deferred, allowing the buyer to ascertain the absence of hidden defects. Such defects, which could determine the termination of the contract, included vision problems, the onset of cramps, as well as the animal's tendency to kick or butt. During the sale, the buyer carried out a careful general inspection of the animal and the mouth was always checked, to verify its age based on the eruption and wear of the permanent teeth. Furthermore, particularly in seedstock, the palate and tongue, up to the node, had to be black. With regard to slaughter cattle, the buying and selling of animals took place both on the markets and in the stables and the butchers, exponents of a dense network of butcher shops once scattered throughout the territory, traditionally bought the animals paying for them by live weight and demonstrating a particular skill in visually estimating the weight. This art, developed and maintained with practice, also involved evaluating the state of fattening of the subject through manual control of the adipose tissue in correspondence with the so-called "keys". The latter corresponded to the tip of the breast, the rib, the stifle, the loins and the tailhead.
