For an accurate estimate of the weight "by sight" it was necessary to respect certain warnings, taking into account, in addition to the conformation of the animal and its state of fattening, also the height of the stands, or the proximity of the animal being negotiated to other larger or smaller animals, situations that could have led to error. At the time of loading to the slaughterhouse, which usually took place early in the morning, the animal had to have fasted since the previous evening. Sometimes the contract stipulated that after slaughter, especially in the case of adult cattle, the farmer would be entitled to a predetermined quantity of meat for broth.

Solidarity between neighbors

Another element of peasant life that is worth dwelling on concerns the solidarity that once widely characterized, in the countryside, the relationships between neighbors, who helped each other in case of difficulty, for example during problematic calvings, or even by taking turns lending each other their cattle during agricultural work. In some properties, a fund was also established, in which all the farmers participated, with a share each, and which was used to compensate for the damage caused by the death of an animal. Leopoldo Tosi himself, immediately after renting the Tenuta Torlonia, took out an insurance policy that protected the sharecroppers in the event of accidents. Unfortunately, the relationships between owners and sharecroppers were not always characterized by such sensitivity and were sometimes painful, to the point of determining the termination of the relationship.

The collapse of consistencies

As is clear from these notes, the references to the flat areas of Romagna have been predominant up to now because it is there that the breed, after being established, developed in its best expression, giving life to its greatest sires and proposing the model from which the current one evolved. After Tosi's successes in Paris at the beginning of the century, with the arrival of Medoro, between the two world wars, the center of gravity of the breed moved to the plains of Ravenna and Forlì while, after the Second World War, it was the areas of Bologna and Cesena that offered many of the sires that allowed us to overcome the critical issues related to chondrodysplasia. Between the end of the Second World War and the early 1970s, while the Romagnola was definitively transformed into a meat breed and was appearing on the international stage, the conditions in which the breed currently finds itself were taking shape. The progressive mechanization of agriculture, the economic boom, industrialization with the associated flight from the countryside, the end of sharecropping, the spread of fruit growing, with the transformation of the farm from traditional rotation to monoculture, the change in customs, the hegemony of large-scale distribution, the wild importation of cattle and meat from everywhere, the lack of generational turnover; all this and more is at the root of the collapse in numbers that has characterized the breed throughout its recent history. It was clear since the 1970s that not only the small farm in the plains, with its nucleus of a few animals, would have no future, but that even closed-cycle breeding of beef cattle in the plains would be at risk. The Romagnola breed would have therefore gradually disappeared from the plain, retreating towards the hilly and mountainous area south of the Via Emilia, where the different vocation of the farms and the grazing breeding system would have contributed to the containment of production costs. The development of the so-called "cow-calf line" would have had to produce weaned calves to be sent to the fattening farms of the plain, where the fertile and irrigated land would have guaranteed the availability of corn for fattening. The plain, holding the highest quality cattle, would have contributed by providing the seedstock to the breeders of the hills, necessary for the consolidation of their herds. This potentially virtuous scheme has been hindered by many factors of a socio-economic, mercantile, speculative, political, opportunistic, and even xenophilic nature, the examination of which would take us too far afield. It can be said that the selection towards maximum productivity, known as "functionalism", which prevailed in the years between the 60s and the 80s of the 20th century, heavily influenced livestock farming, based on the assumption that only the most productive breeds, of all species of livestock interest, were worthy of being raised, to the detriment of native breeds, defined as obsolete and less competitive. This aberration has taken on the tones of barbarism, resulting in the massacre that has led to the extinction, or reduced to the state of relics, of many breeds, even important ones, of all the livestock species raised in Italy. For the Romagnola breed, this has meant the collapse of the numbers, which, from 530,000 heads in 1953, have gone down to just 8,691 heads today (Anabic 2024 data). A similar trend, which has unfortunately also characterized other countries in Southern Europe, as well as parts of Africa, Asia and South America, led the FAO to predict, in 1981, that if this status had been maintained, barely twenty breeds would have remained to dominate world cattle farming, since the first decades of the new millennium. The ones that have been sacrificed on the altar of productivity are mainly the “native” breeds, and the loss in terms of biodiversity, considering that these are ancient ethnic groups, selected for centuries by the environment in which they developed, has been enormous to date. Characteristics such as rusticity, longevity, fertility, resistance to high and low temperatures, the effectiveness of thermoregulation mechanisms, resistance to parasites, the ability to live in arid or semi-arid environments, developing efficient systems of water recovery and exploitation of foods with low nutritional value, often the heritage of native breeds, could be lost forever. And alongside these important resources, not only the beauty of biodiversity would disappear, but also a historical and cultural fabric, developed by the various species over centuries of contact with man.

Romagnola ever greener

In current times, sensitivity towards these problems has increased, the mapping of bovine DNA, genomic selection and genetic-based prophylaxis of diseases and genetic defects have become tools of common use. However, the threats do not cease.

In the era of industrial civilization, global warming and climate change, cattle are being blacklisted and criminalized as major producers of greenhouse gases. Ruminant breeding has been active in this regard for several years, investigating not only the amount of carbon dioxide and methane produced by livestock, but also the composition and variations of their rumen microbiota, in an attempt to build livestock that are increasingly efficient in enhancing food resources. Even the denigrating attacks relating to the damage to health resulting from the consumption of red meat are instrumental in supporting enormous economic interests, which aim to influence consumption on a global scale. The promotion of synthetic meat is just one example. In the age of technology, the internet and globalization, mankind would not lack the tools needed to build a better future. But there is no ethics, or historical knowledge or even respect behind a steak that comes out of a 3D printer and it certainly will not be the last aberration we will see. Even the disruption of the territory, to which increasingly violent meteorological events are unfortunately accustoming us, as well as the plague of fires, can be contained, or even prevented, by the grazing of livestock and the presence of man on the territory. We forget that livestock has been one of the main promoters of civilization and human aggregation. Roads, villages and cities have arisen along the transhumance routes and history has walked in the footsteps of livestock. This socio-cultural bond with the territory is also expressed through the particular richness of our agri-food sector. Yet, once the emergency has passed, these concepts, flaunted instrumentally when necessary, are forgotten until the next catastrophe. The mouths that, in the 70s, preached that local beef cattle breeding, considered uncompetitive, should cease to be replaced with live or dead cattle imported from other European countries, are the same ones that today are exaggerating in favor of biodiversity and excellent production, as if a whitewash of the sarcophagus was enough to redeem them. And yet the absurdities born from delirious minds, sometimes considered authoritative, have made converts and the history of animal husbandry can boast a large sample of them. Only a little more than a century has passed between the Parisian successes obtained by Tosi in 1900 and the present times, but it has been an incredible time span for the importance of the events that have passed through it and that has seen humanity literally leap from the plow to the moon. The decrease in numbers, which the breed has experienced since the end of the 1960s and which currently sees it on the brink of the abyss, has seemed unstoppable, despite the institutions, the Emilia Romagna Regional Authority and the European Community in particular, having tried to stem it with repeated interventions.

Towards what future?

Once its golden age was over, the Romagnola has seen the most passionate, capable and competent figures gradually leave the field to a plethora of characters who too often turned out to be inconsistent, opportunistic, lacking in knowledge, depth and passion. A motto says that nothing important in the world has been built without passion. The Romagnola entrusts its future to the passion, tenacity, sensitivity and intuition of those who breed it today, so that it can continue to enrich the environmental and human context that has accompanied its history and to which it itself has given a fundamental contribution.

Between 1800 and the first half of the 20th century, the Romagnola breeding area included a host of stud farms, mostly public and to a lesser extent private, scattered throughout the region. These "stations" were staffed with recognized and certified breeding stock. This activity was regulated by specific laws, overseen by veterinarians and the then-current "agrarian committees." The breeders themselves were grouped into provincial associations that dictated the guidelines of the activity and established the minimum stud fees. A note by Giorgio Golinelli, regarding the districts of Molinella and S. Pietro Capofiume, in the Bologna area, gives an idea of ​​how numerous public bull stations were: - Suffice it to say that in 1931 alone, in the municipality of Molinella there were 34 "bull stations" (20 of which were public and 14 private) and that a total of 40 bulls were "approved" for this function (of which 25 served at public stud farms and 15 at private ones). Molinella ranked fifth in the provincial rankings in this field, preceded only by Imola, S. Giovanni in Persiceto, Budrio, and Medicina. - This aside gives an idea of ​​how widespread their presence was throughout the area and how they satisfied the need of breeders to be able to take their cows there in times before the advent of mechanization, when livestock movement was done on foot or with the use of animal-drawn vehicles. Subsequently, stud farms provided their own vehicles for transporting the cows, the cost of which was usually included in the stud fee. Beginning in the 1930s, with the establishment of the Herd Book, the activity of bull breeding stations was more strictly regulated, becoming a cornerstone of selection activity. In fact, each of the stud farms developed and maintained active, within its own area of ​​influence, certain sirelines, giving life to the mosaic that contributed to the genetic variability of the breed. From the early 1950s, the emergence and spread of artificial insemination (AI), initially practiced using fresh, refrigerated semen, led some of the breeding stations to convert into Artificial Insemination (AI) Centers, each with its own network of contact details and veterinarians to whom the semen was delivered a couple of times a week. Subsequently, during the 1970s, with the breed in sharp demographic decline and the consolidation of semen freezing techniques, the number of natural service stations and most semen production centers rapidly and progressively decreased until Law No. Law 30 of January 15, 1991, which regulates animal reproduction, did not decree its definitive closure. It is undeniable that artificial insemination has played a fundamental role both in the genetic improvement of livestock and in the prevention of infectious diseases and the health protection of the herds. At the same time, alongside the progressive closure of bull studs, artificial insemination has also led to a gradual increase in average relatedness within the breed. Currently, there are fewer than a dozen bovine semen production centers throughout Italy, and those storing and marketing semen from native Italian beef breeds can be counted on one hand. To ensure the necessary genetic variability of the different ethnic groups, the National Breed Associations have established their own semen collection and storage centers. In the case of Anabic, the semen production center has been active since 2009.
